core: Working definition of research methods as the systematic approaches psychologists use to gather evidence (attributed)

The five named methods: surveys, case studies, naturalistic observation, correlational studies, experiments (one line, original example, one honest limitation each; experiments treated as a sibling topic)
Choosing a method: the research question shapes the method
Samples and populations: who is studied, representativeness
Honest note: every method has blind spots
Honest framing: methods are lenses, not mirrors
supporting: Scientific knowledge is empirical — grounded in observable evidence
Practical constraints (time, money) also shape method choice
outOfScope: Correlation coefficients and statistics (own sibling topic: correlation)
The scientific method in psychology (own sibling topic)
Longitudinal and cross-sectional designs, archival research (mentioned only in passing, not taught)

claims.claim: Psychologists have many research methods available in their efforts to understand, describe, and explain behavior and the cognitive and biological processes that underlie it; each method has unique strengths and weaknesses and may only be appropriate for certain research questions.
Scientific knowledge is empirical: it is grounded in objective, tangible evidence that can be observed and checked, which distinguishes research from intuition and personal experience.

A case study focuses on one person or just a few individuals and yields a depth of information unmatched by other single methods, but the studied individuals are often unusual, which limits generalization to the larger population.

Naturalistic observation means observing behavior in its natural setting; observers must be unobtrusive because people behave less naturally when they know they are being watched, and the approach offers little control over when or whether the behavior occurs.

Surveys are lists of questions answered by research participants, delivered on paper, electronically, or verbally; they make it easy to collect data from large samples, but the information is limited by problems associated with self-reported data.

A sample is a subset of individuals selected from a population, the overall group of individuals the researchers are interested in; researchers study the sample and seek to generalize their findings to the population.

Correlational studies measure variables as they naturally occur and can describe relationships between variables, but correlational data cannot be used to make claims about cause-and-effect relationships; only experiments can support causal claims.
The choice of research method depends on the type of question being asked and on available resources, and because all methods have limitations, the best research uses a variety of methods.

conflictingEvidence.issue: No material conflicts across sources on the evergreen definitions and tradeoffs of the five methods.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e (2.2) describes the same method categories, strengths, and weaknesses as the Noba Project's Research Designs module.
Noba emphasizes practical constraints (time, money) in method choice; OpenStax emphasizes question fit — the two accounts are complementary, not contradictory.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both accounts were used; the lesson states both the question-fit principle and the resource-constraint point, each attributed to the corresponding source.

rightsIssues: OpenStax and Noba pages are used as reference-only verification; no source wording is reproduced in the lesson, and all examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: 2.1 Why Is Research Important? — Psychology 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. openstax.org blocks direct fetching, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2023id_/) of the canonical URL, which serves the full section text. Supports: the goal of psychologists to understand behavior and its underlying cognitive and physiological processes; scientific knowledge as empirical — grounded in objective, tangible evidence observable regardless of who observes; the contrast with intuition and personal experience. Used to verify the empirical framing of the working definition of research methods.

sourceRecords.title: 2.2 Approaches to Research — Psychology 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. openstax.org blocks direct fetching, so the section was read via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2023id_/) of the canonical URL, which serves the full section text. Supports: the working definition (psychologists have many research methods in their efforts to understand, describe, and explain behavior); unique strengths and weaknesses of each method; case studies (one person or a few individuals, unmatched depth, limited generalizability because cases are unusual); naturalistic observation (behavior in its natural setting, unobtrusive observers, people behave differently when watched, little control, observer bias); surveys (lists of questions, paper/electronic/verbal delivery, large samples, self-report problems); sample and population definitions and generalization; correlational methods cannot establish cause and effect; experiments provide control but are often artificial and some questions cannot be studied experimentally for ethical reasons. Backbone source for the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Research Designs
sourceRecords.provider: Noba Project (Christie Napa Scollon, Singapore Management University)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per this subject's source-map (nobaproject.com is live; page read directly 2026-08-22). Supports: the principle that which method you choose depends on the type of questions you are asking and what resources are available; surveys reaching large numbers of people at low cost and with low participant time commitment; correlational designs measuring variables as they naturally occur versus experiments that allow causal inferences; all methods have limitations, which is why the best research uses a variety of methods; practical tradeoffs (time, money) in method selection, including starting with cheaper exploratory methods. Used to verify the question-shapes-method principle and the honest-note framing.
